channel.title: sgit.ai articles
channel.description: Articles and desk notes from sgit.ai, newest first.

item.title: The graphs books: three books written by agents in a day, the altitudes, the board and the book as a graph, what they got right, and why they stopped under review
item.description: In August, on graphs.sgit.ai, agents wrote three books from a month of work on fractal semantic graphs, about 100,000 words between them, because I had a long flight the next day and wanted something to read. I read them, printed, and made a lot of notes. They are good, and much of what is in them, and in how they were made, now runs this newsroom. But two months later they are still at v0.3.0, v0.2.0 and v0.1.0, under review or held. This is the story of those books: what each one argues; the experiments around them, from an altitude ladder that compresses a book into one paragraph and lets you climb back down, to a board of workstreams and a book decomposed to the word and rebuilt byte-identical; why the book about making books read far better than the book about graphs; and where it stopped, which is the most useful part. The change-control workflow designed to apply my review notes had seven stages, and the approve stage was me. Nothing ever passed through it. It is the clearest example I have of a workflow that moves fast while there is energy and then stops, because the next step is too big, and it is why the next books will be made from articles.

item.title: Books from articles: why my books stall at 95%, why these articles do not, and a plan to turn them into books by Web Summit
item.description: I have left a lot of books behind. On Leanpub there are ten, and most stop between 60% and 95% complete; in August, agents wrote three more on graphs.sgit.ai in a day, about 100,000 words, which I read on a long flight, and two months later they are still under review. The reason is the same every time. A book is one big batch: by the time the first version exists, every change is expensive, the review piles up on one person, and when my energy moves to the next place of highest leverage, the book stays behind. The articles on this site work the other way. Each one is researched, checked, released and read on the day, links to what is already written instead of repeating it, and comes back with feedback while it still matters. So here is my hypothesis: a book is a curated, ordered set of finished articles, plus the editorial thread that connects them, and the workflow that makes the articles can make the books. The test is close. Web Summit is in Lisbon from 9 to 12 November, and I would like to have books there: one on agents with a mandate, one on graphs, a new Hacking Portugal, and one on making books this way. This article maps the plan, the material we already have, and what has to be true for it to work.

item.title: The value of constraints: what client-side encryption and open source actually gave us, which is not what you would think
item.description: The value I get from two of sgit's design choices is not the obvious one. sgit is encrypted on the client, and we often lead with that, but I made that mistake myself: nobody will buy sgit for its encryption. If it succeeds, it will be because it has better features and better workflows, and many of those came from the encryption, as a constraint. Encryption on the client moves the security problem from protecting all the data to protecting the keys, and moves the sovereignty line from where the data is stored to who holds the keys; the European Data Protection Board treats that as an effective measure for transfers. It does not take you out of GDPR, which my memo said it did: the data is still personal data for whoever holds the keys, but a breach of the ciphertext alone need not be notified to the people in it. The biggest benefit, though, is engineering. A server that cannot read the data removes the temptation to process anything on it, so there is no server code to write, deploy and secure, and the features that make sgit good, like scoped clones, came from working within that. Open source is the same kind of constraint: no private code removes the temptation to lock customers in, makes the code easy to deploy anywhere, and ends the startup curse of building every customer's integration. That is why it has to be all of it; open core is an evaluation version. The business model that follows is selling customisation.

item.title: Software vendors should become villagers and town planners: let users explore on top of the product, sell them the maintenance of what they build, and use Firefox as the example of what happens if you don't
item.description: I am reaching a point where every piece of software that gets in my way is not just annoying, it is a little offensive, because I know that I could rebuild the part I need. I could make my own version of a browser that behaves exactly as I want. What stops me is not building it; it is maintaining it. That is the opportunity software companies are missing, and I think it is why they should be worried. My argument is a positioning one, in Simon Wardley's terms: a software company should stop thinking of itself as the explorer that invents features, and become the villager and town planner underneath its users, who explore on top of the product, by talking to it, while the company sells them the maintenance of what they built and learns from it. I could not find anyone making this argument; the nearest are Ink & Switch's essay on malleable software and Wardley's own model of innovating on a commodity. Firefox is the example. I came back to it and found a good browser that I could not bend: on the desktop its compact mode was hidden for five years, until Firefox 157 brought it back on 29 September, and on the iPad there is still no way to hide the toolbar. Mozilla's revenue is about 73% royalties, mostly from one customer. I would pay Firefox instead, a pound, ten pounds, fifty, for my version, kept working. The sell-off in software stocks in February, and a developer's open-source clones of seven Adobe applications this month, are early signs of what happens to companies that do not make that move.

item.title: Explorer coding: a better name for what people call vibe coding, what it is good for, and the handover to villagers and town planners before anyone depends on it
item.description: I would like to propose a better name for what is usually called vibe coding: explorer coding. Vibe coding sounds as if people are just typing and ad-libbing, and I have never liked it, because what they are doing is the best thing to happen to software since the spreadsheet: everyone with a need can now explore it by building, with the fast feedback loop that made spreadsheets win, and what they build is the best brief anyone will ever write. Explorer is Simon Wardley's word for exactly that kind of work. It also makes the limit clear. An explorer-coded app may look and feel like an application, but nobody has read the code or checked the architecture, and it is not ready to be in line: once other people depend on it, it is mission critical, and it needs villagers to maintain it, with agent behaviour policies, data handling and releases that do not break it, and then town planners who own the code in production and are accountable for it, as the Linux kernel, Fedora and GitHub already say the human who ships code must be. The further towards commodity, the fewer agents in line and the more deterministic code. And it suggests a commercial model: every product should have an explorer version, where users reshape it by talking to it, and paid conversions from there to a villager product and a town planner one.

item.title: A custom Firefox of my own: the full plan to build one with a governed agent hive, for the laptop and the iPad, and how Mozilla could sell me the part I do not want to do, which is keeping it working
item.description: The previous articles argued that software vendors should let users explore and sell them the maintenance of what they build. This is the practical version, for the product I used as the example: a plan to make a custom Firefox with the workflow we showed at the agentics talk, a Ruflo hive of Claude Code workers, an sgit vault as its memory and a behaviour policy as its mandate, and to run it on my laptop and my iPad. The plan puts each thing I want on the least invasive layer that can deliver it: enterprise policies, hidden preferences, a stylesheet for the browser's own interface, an extension, and only then a patch set on Firefox's source, built in a mode that skips the C++ compile. The iPad is different: Apple requires WebKit, Firefox for iOS is a separate Swift codebase, and the only route is a fork of it, installed with a developer account. The plan works, and it shows where the cost is. Since September Firefox ships every two weeks, so a fork has to be rebased 26 times a year, on two codebases. I can have the hive do that, but it is exactly what I would pay Mozilla to do. Mozilla now sells a branded build and custom development to organisations; I think it should sell the same to one person: explore for free, keep it working for about 50p a release, a change built properly for £50 to £500.

item.title: Agentics, ready to sell: what we showed at Agentic Engineering Live, who else is selling agentic services and at what price, the engagement path, and a marketplace for the consultants who deliver it
item.description: After Thursday's talk at Agentic Engineering Live in London, I think we are ready to sell this. The talk ran itself, twenty-six slides on a clock, most of them live pages that animated their own explanation, and the whole thing was built by the method it described: a Ruflo hive whose workers were Claude Code subagents, an sgit vault per run that kept everything they made, encrypted and versioned, and Agent Behaviour Policies that say what each role may do. ruv.sgit.ai has the five articles written straight after it, the talk, and four offers with published prices. So this article maps the market before we go into it. Who else sells agentic services: the big consultancies with agent platforms, the model vendors with partner networks and forward-deployed engineers, Cognitum with its own four-week discovery, and boutiques selling £2,500 audits and €2,900 sprints. Where the gap is: Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027 for cost, unclear value or weak risk controls. Our position is the evidence: every run leaves a vault and a ledger the client keeps. The engagement path starts with a run and two hours of expert time, and grows to a four-day pilot and a maintained setup. And the delivery needs people, so the last part is a marketplace for consultants: Mondweep Chakravorty, co-founder of the Agentics Foundation's London chapter, and I are the first two; this is the invitation to the rest of the community, with the onboarding we propose.

item.title: Scion and sgit: Anthropic rebuilt source control for agents inside one company, and an open-source encrypted version already does much of the same thing outside it
item.description: On 13 October Anthropic described Scion, the system that replaced Git for its monorepo after merges grew from about 2,500 a day in May to more than 30,000 in September, most of them by Claude. Git's offline, full-clone design, its post says, "was actively undermining our ability to scale", because nearly every client is now an always-online agent or job. Scion moves the work to the server, fetches only what a job needs, and serves immutable objects from three tiers of cache. Reading it, I recognised most of the ideas, because sgit, the encrypted version control we build in the open, arrived at many of them from the other direction. Its object ids are immutable content addresses, so objects cache for a year at a CDN; its server is a dumb store that cannot read what it holds, so reads can come from any static host; and its latest releases add scoped, shallow and on-demand clones. This site's agent checked each claim against sgit 0.22.0's code and measured it on a real vault: a scoped clone in 4 seconds against 59 for the full one, and a full clone served by a plain file server with no sgit server at all. The differences are real too. Scion does history, blame and merges on the server, and runs at a scale sgit has never been tested at; sgit does them on the client, has no blame or bisect yet, and does no packing on the server. But Scion is internal and, in Anthropic's words, "by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use". sgit is open source and on PyPI today, and it encrypts everything.

item.title: Inside the Mesa Ranch desk: a page-by-page tour of an observation vault, from the cover to the knowledge graph you can play in time
item.description: The Mesa Ranch observation desk is a vault with a lot in it, and for someone who has never opened a vault it is hard to get the full reading of it at a glance. So this is the tour. The desk turns Francesco Marconi's INMA deck, When journalism becomes intelligence, into seventeen pages on synthetic records: the argument, in three pages that follow his first slides; the system, as actors, an atlas of 78 event types and an ontology; the record, as seventeen observations, the AI workflow stepped through one real cycle, the journalists' three queues and a community impact tracker; and five graphs of the same knowledge, including a fractal semantic graph that opens level by level from the question to the records, and a knowledge graph you can play one observation at a time. Every page has the same frame: a menu on the left, the page in the middle, and a panel on the right where anything you click opens with the evidence behind it. This article walks through each page: what it shows, what to click, and what it proves; and it ends with how to open the vault yourself, clone it and rebuild it for your own beat.

item.title: When journalism becomes intelligence, built: an observation desk for one data-center buildout, from an atlas of 78 events to a community impact tracker, in a vault you can open
item.description: Francesco Marconi shared the slides of an INMA talk with a line I agree with completely: "As AI makes content production easier, journalism's competitive advantage will increasingly come from how we observe the world." His deck makes it concrete with a data-center buildout in the desert: journalism as delta science, a map of who wants what, an atlas of events each with a definition and an observable signal, a domain ontology, observations that add to what the newsroom knows, a workflow of observe, compare, check, report and update, and a community impact tracker. I wanted to see it working, so this site's agent built it: a vault on this site, an app of seventeen pages that follows the eleven slides, runs each one on real data structures, and adds five graphs of the same knowledge. The atlas has all 12 families and 78 event types; the ontology has six entities and six relationships; sixteen source records produce seventeen observations, each a subject, a change, a time and its evidence; and the tracker turns them into an article and two alerts. The records are synthetic, on purpose: a fictional campus in a fictional county, because fake permits under real agencies' names would be exactly the kind of record a newsroom like this should never publish. The method is the point, and a vault is a natural home for it: the observation history is a versioned record, the evidence travels with every claim, and anyone with the read key can open it, check it, and copy it for their own beat.

item.title: Your own newsroom: how a founder can tell their story by voice memo, with an agent that checks it and publishes it to GitHub Pages, and readers who pay a little if they find it useful
item.description: The founders I most want to see succeed are the authentic ones, the people who come from the field they are building for. Their brand is themselves, and they need a medium for it: a place that keeps their history, what they do, their stories, their struggles, their ideas, their path and their milestones, so that they remember it and others can find it. This site is written that way. I record a voice memo, an agent session wired to GitHub researches it, checks every claim, writes it in my voice and publishes it to a static site, and readers pay a few pence a page if they find it useful. Everything needed to do the same exists today. This is the recipe, step by step: one public GitHub repository; GitHub Pages, published by GitHub Actions after a validation step; a Claude plan with cloud sessions and the Claude GitHub App, used from a browser or a phone; a house-rules file the agent reads first; the reader meter from api.newsroom.sgit.ai, pinned to a release, with a Stripe Payment Link you own; and the habits that make it trustworthy: corrections in the open, sources at the end, and nothing confidential in a public repository. It is simpler than this newsroom, and it does not need to be called a newsroom. It is also a good way to learn, in a native way, what publishing a pure client-side site actually means.

item.title: The expert founders: why the next startups will be built by the people who know the problem, and why Europe's slower, sceptical money suits them
item.description: For twenty years the winning technology startup was usually built by a clever, ambitious outsider: someone who found a pain point, often through a hundred conversations with people they could reach, raised money on belief, hired the subject-matter experts, and displaced incumbents that had the customers, the knowledge and sometimes the money. It is a very American playbook, many bets for a few large wins, and it changed whole industries. It also has a second act: the disruptors became the incumbents, and much of what they built is now the software everyone complains about. My argument is that generative AI changes who can start. When agents do most of the execution, the people who know the problem can build the product themselves, without the millions that used to come first. The data on experts was always on their side: the fastest-growing US startups are founded at a mean age of 45, and three or more years in the same industry doubles the rate of top-tier success. And this favours Europe: its investors want to see it working, value lower, and ask for more revenue at the raise, which is exactly the discipline an expert founder needs, because money too early is one of the most reliable ways to kill a startup. Three examples: me in security, a knee surgeon in knee health, and a transcriber in legal transcription.

item.title: Omnichannel programming: briefs by voice, reviews by voice, previews on the phone, and one shared state underneath, at every stage from explorer to town planner
item.description: I no longer program in one place. I brief in a voice memo while walking, review a draft by voice, check the preview on my phone, test on the computer, read the pull request on GitHub, and pick the same work up on an iPad. Retail has a word for this. In 2011 Darrell Rigby wrote in Harvard Business Review that successful companies would engage customers through omnichannel retailing, and the difference that made the word stick is the one that matters here: multichannel means separate channels, each with its own copy of the work; omnichannel means every channel reads and writes one shared state. For programming, that state is git, vaults, briefs and graphs. This site is the worked example: in three days, one agent session took 54 messages from me, 10 of them voice memos, and turned them into 40 releases, 36 articles and 87 figures, with research, hooks, tests and other agents working in the same repository. It works at every stage of a Wardley map, for explorers, villagers and town planners, and at every altitude, from intent down to the code, including code review. It is already how a new generation of developers and founders works. And it breaks in known ways, which the shared state is there to fix.

item.title: secrets.sgit.ai on public keys: no more shared keys, eight ways a secret moves, a vault for the private key, and the commercial service it becomes
item.description: secrets.sgit.ai started on 5 October as the MVP of a password manager unlocked by a passkey, and it is a good example of our non-linear path: its passkey work became the reader's vault on this newsroom, and its own app was never built; its reality page lists 42 claims shipped, all of them the site, the pipeline and the labs, and the app itself as proposed. Now I want to turn it into a commercial service for one job: moving a secret from A to B. The principle is to stop sharing keys altogether. We tried keys that were easy to use, and the sgit team's own security review found them broken: about 30 bits, a public id that is an unsalted hash of the key, and one precomputed table that opens every one; the command line team disabled creating them in June. So everything moves to public-key cryptography, which the pieces we already have support. Every person, browser and agent has a key pair; the public key is shared freely, by link, QR code, email or WhatsApp; the secret comes back encrypted to it, as a one-time drop, a file or a QR code; and the private key lives in a vault of its own, unlocked by a passkey that Google Password Manager or iCloud Keychain keeps. This site's agent tested the parts that matter: an agent's key pair and a one-time drop, end to end; and a browser key that cannot be exported, which survived a restart and still decrypted. Eight scenarios, what exists for each, what to build, and what to charge for.

item.title: Handing secrets to agents and browsers: SG/Send's next focus, a key pair where the work runs, one-time drops, and a brief for a site that does only this
item.description: The pain I have right now is giving secrets to the places that do my work: vault keys to a browser where the passkey does not reach, and vault keys to the agent sessions I schedule every day. Copying them by hand is slow and risky, and when I tell an agent in its prompt that something is a secret to be careful with, it sometimes refuses to use it at all. So I want SG/Send's technology to focus on one use case: handing a secret, or a public key, to an agent or a browser, as a separate site, mostly client-side, with a command line. The back end already has most of what this needs: a transfer that can be downloaded once and then deleted, an expiry, and client-side encryption; it does not, I found, restrict by location, which I thought it did. The design flips the usual direction: the recipient makes its own key pair where it runs and shows only the public half, by QR code, link or paste; the owner encrypts the secret to it and signs it; the drop is read once; and the secret goes from the drop into the tool, never into the chat. This site's agent ran it end to end on a local server: the agent decrypted the secret, the second download got a 410, the owner's signature verified once the agent knew the owner's key, and a browser made a key pair it refused to export. The industry is moving the other way, keeping secrets out of agents entirely; for an encrypted vault that cannot work, because the key has to reach the place that decrypts.

item.title: My memory, checked: thinking out loud in a voice memo, publishing only what the record supports, and why peer review has moved to before publishing
item.description: Something has changed in how I write, and I only noticed because I now take it for granted. When I record a voice memo for an article, I say things the way I remember them, in the order I remember them, with the instinct ahead of the evidence. Then the agent that writes with me goes and checks: the repositories, the commits, the briefs, the documentation, the web, and my own old writing. In the last eight articles, five of my claims were confirmed, five were corrected and two could not be found, and the articles say which. I first saw this with ChatGPT Deep Research, which launched in February 2025: eight days later, an essay I wrote with it about the O2 Platform cited three of my own blog posts from 2012, thirty-one times, as its evidence. It changes three things. Peer review used to come after publishing, from whoever on Twitter or LinkedIn noticed the mistake; now it comes before. Thinking out loud, which used to drive my teams mad as a plan moved from Monday to Friday, is now safe, because the record catches up with the instinct. And every article carries its provenance, so journalists, researchers and their agents can check it again, and rewrite it in their own voice.

item.title: From sending a file to sgit: eight months of SG/Send, told by its own briefs and commits, and how a file-sharing service became encrypted version control and vaults
item.description: SG/Send started because sending a file was harder than it should be, and because I wanted to build a service where the server holds nothing: the best way to protect an asset is not to have one. Eight months later it has become sgit, encrypted version control with Git's model, and the vaults that this site runs on. The whole journey is in public repositories, so this time I asked this site's agent to check my memory against the record: 4,476 commits on the SG/Send app on 246 of its first 249 days, 1,620 on the sgit command line, 739 release tags, 1,389 brief files and 268 debriefs. The record changes the order I remembered. The vault and the data room were named in February, before folders, zips and Git; the first feature a paying user asked for went from proposal to production in 22 minutes; the move to Git's model took about two weeks of briefs and a simulation that found 14 gaps before any code was written. It also shows the pace: fast from February to May, a turn to focus in June, two long pauses on the command line, and a burst in October. And it shows the lesson: by 5 March the briefs already said "Users buy credits, test once, and don't come back." The technology worked. The use case was not there yet.

item.title: The scripted talk: a presentation as a timeline that plays on a clock, the two vaults it grows out of, and a player built for tonight's ten minutes
item.description: I usually give a talk by reading it, with the slides behind me. For a short slot tonight I want to try something else: a talk that is completely scripted, where the slides, the builds, the animations and even the demo play on a clock, and I speak to them instead of reading from them. This grows out of two talks already published as vaults on sgit.ai. The Black Hat Europe 2025 keynote made the slides data: 26 slides in one JSON file that the app reads at load time, with ten versions of the slide system beside it. The VoiceDebrief pitch added a presenter with per-slide timings, a countdown and speaker notes, built from a template by a script. The next step is to make the whole talk a timeline. This site's agent built a first version: one HTML file that plays a file of beats, each with a start, a duration, a slide and the words to say, with builds, a terminal that types a command and prints its recorded output, tables that reveal row by row, video, and a presenter view with the words, the seconds left and what comes next. A rehearsal mode records planned against actual times. The first timeline is the five-minute demo for ruv.sgit.ai, the newest site in the sgit family, built for tonight's Agentic Engineering Live with rUv in London. And Claude Motion, which Anthropic released in beta on 8 October, makes the animations the same way: as code, exported as MP4.

item.title: The tokens hook: a token behaviour policy that shows what every session reads, caches, writes and costs, why a prompt cannot do it, and a brief for tokens.hook.sgit.ai
item.description: It is easy to spend a lot of money on model calls without seeing where it goes, and the user is the person who sees least. So I asked for a small, focused agent behaviour policy about tokens: in observe mode first, it should show the user, in a box of ASCII under each answer, how many tokens the session has read, how many came from the cache, how many it wrote, how big the context is and roughly what it has cost. This site's agent built it as a Claude Code hook of 132 lines with a policy file, and tested it. A prompt cannot do this job: asked to report its own usage, the model said twice, correctly, that it could not see the numbers. The hook gave it the exact figures, one turn behind, in about a millisecond. Building it found a bug in our own session report, which had been counting every response two or three times, because the transcript repeats a response's usage on each of its content blocks. It also found that, in this version of Claude Code, the transcript a hook can read carries the system prompt and every tool definition, though the documentation does not say so. This session has read 99% of its input from the cache, which at list prices is the difference between about $170 and about $1,950. The other tools vary: Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor have hooks and usage commands, the chat apps show only limits. And this is the brief for tokens.hook.sgit.ai, a small site for a small, mission-critical piece of code.

item.title: Cedar and the policy vault: a debrief on the policy language agents are adopting, where our behaviour policies and sgit vaults meet it, and a brief for the MVP
item.description: Cedar is the policy language I think we should adopt rather than compete with. AWS open-sourced it in May 2023 under Apache 2.0; it joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a Sandbox project on 8 October 2025; it is the language of Amazon Verified Permissions and of AgentCore Policy, which checks every agent tool call before it runs; and its design is modelled and proved in Lean. That is a mature environment, and it already says most of what our agent behaviour policies say: permit for the grant, forbid for the barrier, a schema for the footprint. What it does not carry is why a rule exists, which version was in force, or the evidence of what it decided. Those are exactly what an encrypted, versioned vault is good at. So I asked this site's agent to try it: Cedar policies, schema, entities and tests in an sgit vault, a gate that refuses any version that fails validation, tags signed by the releasing clone, enforcement points that clone with a read key and cannot write, and an append lane that keeps a sealed, hash-chained record of every decision. It worked on a local server, and it found one thing worth knowing: Cedar skips a policy whose evaluation fails, so a forbid that refers to a missing attribute lets the action through. This article is the debrief, the crosswalk between their terms and ours, and the brief for the agent that will build the MVP.

item.title: The citizen developer is good news: the spreadsheet grown up, the best briefs ever written, and the handover from explorers to villagers and town planners that makes them last
item.description: At a conference today the phrase "citizen developer" came up as a worry, the new name for people outside IT building things they should not. I think it is one of the best things to happen to software, and a better way to talk about what is usually called vibe coding. It is not only citizens: it is the employee, the business owner, the expert, the person who knows the work. People have always built with what they controlled, and for most of them that was a spreadsheet; spreadsheets are full of errors, and the world runs on them anyway, because they were the only tool people had. Now they can build full applications, and those applications are also the best briefs ever written: what the user actually wants, in a form that runs. The work is the handover, from the explorer who built it to the villagers who harden it and the town planners who make it scale, with all the non-functional requirements the explorer never had to think about. Encrypted, versioned vaults are a natural carrier for that: a mini app with its UI and its data in one place, which is what a spreadsheet always was, with history, keys and a clean handover added. Done well, this lets people, organisations and even countries move from rent-seeking, control-based software to tools that serve them, which is also the direction of the business models this newsroom is testing.

item.title: Paying after the value: why a balance that can go negative feels different from a subscription, the psychology behind it, and the experiment this newsroom is running
item.description: Almost every time I buy something, I am buying future value. A subscription, a gym membership, a big security product on a good deal, even a one-off purchase: I am betting that I will use it enough for the price of each use to fall to a number I am comfortable with. Often I lose the bet, and the cost of unsubscribing keeps me paying. The research agrees: gym members on a monthly contract paid more than $17 a visit when they could have paid $10. This newsroom is trying the opposite. You start with £5 of credit, each article you read uses a few pence, you can set the price from free to double or refuse it, and the balance can go below zero and stay there. By the time you are asked to pay, you have the value in front of you: what you read, how much, what you liked. The payment is connected to what you received, not what you hope to receive. That only works where the cost of serving is close to zero, which is true of a static site on a CDN, and where the value adds up in a way the reader can see. Wikipedia is the counter-example: £20 a year asked for at a moment with no value in view, even though it is a few pence an article. Add prices fair by country, the Big Mac index for reading, and a view of where the money goes, and payment becomes a choice people are glad to make. The experiment is live, with written hypotheses and a review in December, and I will report back.

item.title: The eyeballs get cheap: why open source is about to become the most secure software we have, and why secure, sovereign and paid-for meet at the least code in production
item.description: For as long as I have worked in security there has been no clear winner between open source and proprietary software. Open source had the code in view, and fixes that sweep a bug's variants; it also had very few people and almost no budget for the slow, expensive reviews that find the hard bugs. Proprietary software had the budget, and the cover of being hidden, and got away with a lot. That balance just moved. Models can now run deep security reviews over and over, on every project, at a cost that used to buy one consultant for a day. The thing open source lacked was paid attention, and that is the thing that just became abundant. I thought Chainguard had started publishing the projects where its AI found nothing; I could not find that. What I found is better: the maintainer of curl writing about a year in which AI review first drowned his project in noise, then produced hundreds of real fixes, then a frontier scan that found a single low-severity bug, and then, today, deeper tools finding more. That is what a project getting harder to break looks like. Put it next to two things I have argued before, that sovereignty needs open code and open schemas, and that the business is maintaining the version each customer actually runs, and three forces meet at one place: the least amount of code in production.

item.title: Commander's intent is a behaviour policy: Sondera's argument in our words, the business layer above it, and five of our rules compiled to Cedar and tested
item.description: Josh Devon of Sondera published an article today that I think is one of the clearest statements of the problem we keep writing about. Agents do not go rogue; they follow the instructions they were given and fill the gaps with whatever gets the job done. The military solved this a long time ago with commander's intent, the objective and its limits written down together, and agents inherited the initiative and none of the limits. His answer is to write the limits about effects, not actions, compile them into rules a machine can check, and enforce them outside the agent before every action. We are talking about the same thing in different words, so I joined the two vocabularies: twelve of their terms against ours, most of them the same idea, and two places where one side goes further. We go further up, into the business layer, where an agent's limits stop being universal and become how a company does invoices and who it is in dispute with. They go further in proof, compiling plain English into Cedar and checking it with a theorem prover. To show the two halves meeting, I wrote five rules as Cedar, their published example, two from this session's own policy, one from the skill policy I published today and two from our business layer, and evaluated fourteen requests against them. All fourteen came out as intended. The incidents behind their argument check out against Anthropic's and the UK AI Security Institute's own reports, with a few figures rounded differently.

item.title: A skill behaviour policy: what a skill says it does, what it can do, what it is given, and the control that closes the gap, measured on 899 skills
item.description: I saw a video today that said "1 in 20 Claude skills are built to hack your computer". It is an overstatement of a real study, and the real finding is interesting enough: in one large study of public marketplaces, 5.2% of the skills analysed showed "high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent". It made me think about what an agent behaviour policy can do for skills. A skill behaviour policy looks at three things. The mandate the description promises; the mandate the skill actually has, from what its instructions and files can do, treated as features; and the grant, which depends on where it runs. The gap between the first two is the suspicious part; the gap between the last two is the reach nobody asked for. Then the policy becomes a control: a hook and a sandbox setting, generated from the described mandate, that bring the grant down to what you expected. I built a static calculator and ran it on 899 public skills from three sources: 812 can reach something beyond their own scripts, 782 of them through one third-party tool server, and 39 have a feature their description does not mention. None was obfuscated. The clearest case was honest: a skill that reads your Claude Code chat history, searches HackerNews and sends a report to Slack has the whole lethal trifecta, says so, and still needs a control. NVIDIA's scanner rated it safe, which is right for the question a scanner asks. A policy asks a different one.

item.title: sgit in GitHub Actions, side by side: a showcase repository and site that runs four ways of moving a vault between jobs on every run, measured, with a budget for its LLM steps
item.description: sgit in a CI pipeline described how an encrypted vault can carry data in and out of GitHub Actions, and between its jobs. The next step is to show it running, and to keep showing it. So this is a brief for a dedicated repository and website, just for that: its own issues, its own CI pipeline, and on every run four ways of moving a vault between jobs, side by side, in parallel. A vault server with the keys in the repository's secrets; the encrypted vault itself as an artefact, a zip that one job uploads and the next downloads; the vault published as files and cloned read-only from any web host; and append lanes for jobs that only need to hand results in. Each lane reports its time, its bytes, the keys each job held and a screenshot, and repeats on vaults of growing size with full, thin and path clones. I measured the core of it locally for this article. A clone of one folder barely grows with the vault: 0.59 seconds at 100 files, 0.77 at 2,000. A full clone grows with it, from 0.95 to 5.55 seconds. The repository should also have a budget, because some steps will call models, from more than one provider, and every token they spend should be counted against it.

item.title: Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults: seven architectures from one agent to a swarm, a repository of recipes that gates sgit's releases, and what a hundred writers did to an append lane
item.description: There is a pattern I keep using for agents that work together: give them an encrypted vault as their shared memory and their way of talking, and let it exist only for as long as the work does. I want to capture it properly, as a series of architectures from simple to complex, each in a repository of its own with its agents, its keys, its fixtures and a CI job that proves it works, so that people and agents can fork them as templates, recipes and skills. The repository should run as one of the checks before anything reaches sgit's main branch. The key questions are the same at every level: how do you give agents shared memory, how do they communicate, how do they work asynchronously, and how do you know what each one is doing at any moment. The answer depends on who holds which key. Because the only thing that ever leaves the environment is ciphertext, you can be more relaxed about where the logs and the data go: it is all about the keys, and about whether the vault is ephemeral. A vault app can draw what the agents are doing, and the screenshot can go back into the vault. And I wanted to know how far it scales, so we measured it locally: a hundred writers posting ten entries each landed a thousand entries in an append lane in 4.9 seconds, none lost. The same test found four defects, which is the case for the release gate in one paragraph.

item.title: Hooks are kernel code: a maturity model, the first ten hooks mapped, and a brief for a hooks site and feed where you pay for state, never to run
item.description: The hooks we are now going to deploy are code, and very critical code. They are also a very good example of code that is simple in many ways: a hook can be five lines. That makes them the best case study I can think of for everything we do on code review, code practices, semantic graphs and change blast radius, because the problem is small enough to do completely. A hook runs on every matching action, with the user's permissions, and can see, block or rewrite what the agent does; we should treat it like kernel code. Hooks also range from completely deterministic scripts to hooks that call a model or a whole agent, so I propose a maturity model: five levels from the prompt to off the machine, and three questions for every hook, how much power it has, which legs of the lethal trifecta it touches, and how much sandbox it runs in. I mapped the first ten: three this session runs, five tested in a sandbox, two proposed. They are between 4 and 26 lines, and the smallest of them depend on much more: the eleven-line commit hook calls a 37-line scan, so one line changed in the scan moves the commit gate for every session. And this is a brief for a site and a feed to manage them, like a skills manager: every hook from its intent, with its graph, tests, version and signature, installable anywhere, and a billing model where nobody pays to run a hook, but paying buys state.

item.title: Chainguard, mapped: what it builds, what it publishes, how far up the stack its context goes, and where an open behaviour policy and an encrypted vault could plug in
item.description: Chainguard is one of the companies doing the most interesting work in software supply chain security, and much of it is open: the Wolfi distribution, public advisory feeds, Sigstore in its lineage, and a growing set of products for agents. So I mapped it: the company, what it builds from the operating system up to agents, what data it publishes that anyone can read, and how deep that data goes. I read the feeds and counted them. 12,480 advisories covering 12,125 distinct CVEs; in a sample, about seven in ten findings marked fixed and one in five marked as not applying. And in the archived Wolfi advisories, where the reasons were public, 2,850 determinations that a vulnerability did not apply, of which 177 gave a reason about context: the vulnerable code is not in the execution path, an attacker cannot control it, or it is mitigated. That is where the graph stops, and it is the question that matters to me. As with everything in security, it is about context. An image with many vulnerabilities is fine if the application on top never reaches them; one reachable flaw is not. Deciding which images are non-negotiable and which can ship today needs a graph from the user story, through the code and its dependencies, to the container. That context layer is where an open behaviour policy and an encrypted vault fit, next to the agent products Chainguard is now shipping, which already talk about policies. I make the case for each.

item.title: The wire as a graph: start from what the reader sees, give every story and every name a long-lived ID, link every phrase of a short narrative, and a brief for the desks
item.description: The wires already collect the day's news into encrypted vaults on a schedule. This is the next step, and the way to design it is to start at the end, with what the reader sees, and work backwards to the data. A story should read as a short narrative in which every name is a link, to a person, a company, an event or a place, each with a long-lived ID, and every sentence is a claim with its evidence: a fact, an observation, a statement by a party, or our analysis. Stories group into stories, and that is the fractal part: a thread is a story made of stories, and an article someone else published is a story too. From there, the primitives: a run that collects, captures that freeze what was read, claims, stories, stories of stories and names, each with a random ID that never changes. I measured the four wires' public vaults today: 202 stories, 1,358 distinct names, only 171 of them in more than one story and 48 in more than one wire, and only 44% of the names a story lists appear in its own text. Those numbers say where the work is, and how big a folder tree it needs: a name gets its own folder when it has gravity. Earlier experiments that linked every word of a long text were the right idea done too much. A wire story's narrative is about 55 words, small enough to link every phrase. Cheaper models can do the heavy lifting and a more capable one can check it. This article is also the brief for the desks and the wire agent.

item.title: System prompts as behaviour policies: Claude's published prompt and a leaked ChatGPT one, mapped into rows, a taxonomy of rules, and a JSON file a harness could enforce
item.description: I have said before that a system prompt is a light behaviour policy. So I tested it. The hypothesis: can an existing system prompt be represented as an agent behaviour policy, and if so, what should that look like as a JSON file that models can read and harnesses can enforce, with stronger controls in more places than the prompt itself? Anthropic publishes Claude's system prompts, so the test used the real one: Claude Haiku 5.5's, published on 7 October 2026. It holds 4,255 words and 82 rules. Sorted by kind, 36 of them, about tool use, conversation state, referrals, knowledge and input trust, could be held by the harness rather than by the model's good behaviour; 21 harm restrictions could be held in part by classifiers outside the model, which Anthropic already uses; and 25, about judgement and presentation, stay with the model. For contrast, a leaked ChatGPT prompt, unverified, is the opposite shape: about six words in seven sit under its tool sections. Between them they are the two halves of a behaviour policy, the rules and the reach. What neither has is a mandate, a statement of who may override whom that the harness can check, or a record of what keeps each rule. So I propose an ontology and a taxonomy for it, and a JSON shape. And I looked for anyone running a written agent behaviour policy for real: the formats are arriving, the published policies are not.

item.title: The agents write too: lessons, debriefs and a page for every agent on the newsroom, and a brief for the conductor that will keep it
item.description: The newsroom is no longer one agent. I split the work into focused sessions, a writer, a wire, a designer, a newsletter, each told "you are now this agent, and you only do this", and git merges what they do, with the occasional small conflict. That works well, and it has created two problems. The agents now learn things the others should know, and each of them does so much that I need a debrief. So the newsroom gets a new area and a new workflow. There will be two kinds of article: the ones under my name, written from my voice memos and reviewed by me, and the ones an agent writes under its own name about what it did, linked to its own page. Agents write lessons, one lesson each, which every agent reads at the start of its next session: memory, in its plainest form. They write debriefs, which are also the source material for my articles. Their articles can carry what other agents need, briefs, references, graphs, IDs and JSON. A page keeps track of every agent. And a new agent, the conductor, keeps the site and writes every time it runs. Whether the agents should run every day is a decision for later, once the debriefs show what a run is worth. This article is also the brief for the session that builds it.

item.title: Are hooks the sweet spot? Moving an agent's rules from hope into hooks, rule by rule, until enforcement moves off the machine
item.description: Most of the rules we give agents today are hope-based security: written in the prompt, kept only if the model keeps them. The agent writing this site works under a behaviour policy of eleven rules, and only one of them is kept by something other than the agent. So I asked the question directly: in October 2026, are hooks the sweet spot? Can we move the rules out of the prompt and into small deterministic programs the agent's harness runs before and after every action, and keep them there until enforcement moves into a gateway or the platform itself? I took this session's own policy and tried, rule by rule, in a throwaway repository. Four rules moved into hooks fully, two mostly, three partly and two not at all, and the tests found a gap in the check I trust most. Hooks are the first layer that does not rely on the model and the last that still sees the action in the agent's own terms, which is why I think they are the right place to start, provided they are installed where the agent cannot edit them and set to fail closed. The open hook collections that exist block dangerous commands; the step that is missing is generating hooks from a written policy, and testing them, so the same rules can later be enforced by a gateway. We already need this for our own agents, so we can be among its heaviest users.

item.title: Agent hooks in October 2026: a technical debrief on what each platform lets you see, stop and change, where hooks run, and where they fail
item.description: More and more of the technical people I talk to who are trying to control agents for real are reaching for the same tool: hooks, small programs the agent's harness runs at fixed points, before a tool call, after it, when a prompt is submitted, when the agent stops. This is the debrief I wanted to read: the lay of the land on 14 October 2026, from each vendor's own documentation. The short version is that the design has converged. Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf), Grok Build, Factory, Augment and Kiro all offer a hook before a tool call that can block it, and most can ask the user or rewrite the call. They differ where it matters for security: whether an organisation can force its own hooks and switch everyone else's off, whether a failing hook blocks or lets the action through, whether hooks shipped in a repository need trust before they run, and whether anything can see the model's own output. ChatGPT offers admin controls rather than hooks, and Lovable gates publishing rather than agent actions. The vendors and the people who publish hook collections say the same thing about their limits: guardrails, not walls. Hooks see what the harness routes through them, run with the user's permissions, fail open by default on most tools, and have been an attack surface themselves. I ran a small test of my own in a throwaway repository, and the companion article asks what this means for agent behaviour policies.

item.title: Knowledge that maintains itself: semantic graphs for an organisation's policies and internal knowledge, briefing people and agents from the graph, and vaults to carry the brief
item.description: In a conversation today I tried to put in a few sentences what all the graph work on this site is for, and it came out as knowledge management. Take an organisation's policies and internal information, and build a fractal semantic graph of it: an ontology and a taxonomy for every element, each part kept in its own vocabulary, with named edges between them. Then brief people and agents from the graph, not from the pile of documents. They get the slice they need and the diff since they last read it, so the context is there and the tokens are not wasted. It looks a bit like vector search, but vectors give you similarity, not a reason, and the answer can change with the model and the index; a graph gives the same answer to the same question and the path that led to it. The most important part is that the feedback loop maintains itself. You do not have to get the graph right first; you have to maintain it, and agents are very good at maintaining graphs. When something in the graph looks wrong, you ask why, and the answer is a fix at the right altitude. I measured the briefing on this site: the graphs of its 112 articles hold about an eighth of the articles' text. And the brief has to travel. That is what sgit is for: an encrypted git where I give an agent the key to a vault, it reads and writes there, I can scope it to one folder and encrypt to it with its own key, and the vault itself says, this is what you need to read now.

item.title: The minimum code below: container security from the top down, from the user story to the immutable line, measured on one real tool
item.description: A conversation at Chainguard's event today sharpened something I have thought for a while. Chainguard does security from the bottom up, and does it very well: it rebuilds the operating system and the libraries from source, keeps the images minimal and manages the whole process. But even the most locked-down image still holds a great deal of code the application never runs, the assurance still depends on testing, and the loop that caused the problem in the first place is still there: when something breaks, you give it more. As soon as the work reaches the application, it stops. My proposal is to come from the other end. Start from the user story and, at every layer down, ask one question: what is the minimum code below this that the layer above needs? Keep that, remove everything else, and draw the immutable line as high as the evidence allows. It did not scale before; with models and fractal semantic graphs, it can. I measured it for this article on a real tool, sgit and its dependencies, running a CI-style use case under coverage and then running it again from a tree holding only the files that ran. Of 1,500 files, 428 were kept, and the use case passed; commands outside it failed because their code was not there. It also showed the limits: one compiled binary held three quarters of the bytes and no coverage tool can see inside it, and coverage missed a compiled module the tests then caught. Tools that minimise containers at run time already exist, so the new part is the direction: from what the application is for, through a graph, down to a build that can be certified. Chainguard is unusually well placed to offer it, and someone will build it.

item.title: A policy for every skill: Sean Turner's natural-language control for agent skills, the behaviour policy behind it, and using models to need them less
item.description: I was with my friend Sean Turner this week, talking about agent behaviour policies, and he described something he built that I think is great. It is a natural-language control policy for agent skills, and a CI pipeline that checks every skill contributed to an organisation-wide repository against it before hundreds of developers pull it down to their machines. Is it safe, secure, well documented, usable, understandable by the model and understandable by people. And the part that makes it more than a linter: it reads the skill in its context. A skill that turns internal documentation into a LinkedIn post has no untrusted input to worry about; a skill that pulls content off the web is handling untrusted text, and should treat it as data, not obey it. It sits beside a security scan, not instead of one: the question is operational, is this the right way to give this skill to our workforce. That is an agent behaviour policy for a skill: the mandate is what the skill is for, the reach is everything it touches, and the gap is the risk. A control written in natural language is hope-based security, better than nothing and not enough on its own. Sean's next step is the one I keep coming back to: use an agent to write deterministic rules that follow the natural-language control, and keep the description, not the code, as the canonical version. Change the description, regenerate the code. Using models to need them less. And in a common ontology, a whole catalogue of skills becomes one graph, where the dangerous combinations are a query.

item.title: Policy as code needs a policy first: what an agent behaviour policy adds, and how to reverse engineer one from the code, the spreadsheet or the paper you already have
item.description: At an event this week a speaker described policy as code as the way to scale governance and AI innovation together, and it clicked. Policy as code is right, and it is where agent governance has to end up. But for agents it answers one question, is this request allowed, and the questions a business, an auditor or an insurer asks are the ones around it, the ones an Agent Behaviour Policy holds. What can this agent reach, measured. What was it asked to do, and why. Where the two differ. Which rules can no engine ever see. And the one that surprised me when I checked: for every rule that is code, who can change that code. A rule the agent can rewrite is a setting, not a control. Because an ABP has those columns, it can be written in both directions. From the policy, generate code: for this article, five rows of a real ABP became a Rego policy that Open Policy Agent ran against seven requests, denying a push to the wrong repository, a commit without a leak scan and a model id in a diff, asking before a pull request, and allowing a sentence no engine can judge. From what exists, reverse engineer the policy: parse the code back, and the gaps show on both sides, a row with no code and a rule nobody wrote a reason for. I did it to this session's own policy: of its eleven rules, eight have some code behind them, and only one has code the agent cannot change. Fractal semantic graphs are what make the round trip work across paper, spreadsheets, regulations and code, because each keeps its own vocabulary and the edges between them carry verbs both ways.

item.title: sgit in a CI pipeline: encrypted, versioned data in and out of GitHub Actions, between its jobs, through write-only lanes, and a key for every job
item.description: Getting data in and out of a CI pipeline is harder than it should be. GitHub Actions has artifacts, kept 90 days by default and deleted with their run; caches, 10 GB per repository and evicted after a week unused; and job outputs, at most 1 MB per job. Each is fine for its job, and none is a versioned, encrypted record that a person, an auditor or another pipeline can read from outside GitHub. This article maps how sgit vaults fill that gap, and every pattern in it was run for the article against a local vault server. A job pushes what it produced to a vault, and anything with the read key can clone it from anywhere, with history. Jobs pass data to each other through the same vault, each cloning only the folders it needs with --path, which is a large saving in time and in what lands on the runner, though it is a speed setting rather than a boundary. The boundaries are the keys: a read key clones and cannot commit; an append token, one per test shard, adds to its own write-only inbox and reads nothing; and each job can have its own key pair, so a deploy configuration encrypted to the deploy job fails to decrypt anywhere else, and a signed manifest fails verification once it is changed. Even done a little loosely, that turns wiring mistakes into loud failures. The keys come from secrets on stdin, and only the ciphertext half of a vault ever leaves the runner. And when you would rather not depend on a hosted server, the vault server runs as a sidecar whose storage folder holds only ciphertext: archive it into the Actions cache, an artifact or a git branch, and the next run restores it with its full history.

item.title: The homepage is a vault: a fresh edition every morning, every past homepage one commit away, served from plain files, and a brief for the agent that builds it
item.description: The homepage of this site has to be fresh every day, and today it changes only when someone releases the site. I want a job that runs every morning at about 05:45, reads the latest articles, the wires and what is happening in the industry, and writes a new edition of the homepage. And I want that homepage to be a vault. Every edition a commit with a signed tag and its own version line; every edition carrying the links it showed and why, a screenshot of itself and the release note that explains it; any past homepage one commit id away; variants side by side for A/B tests; and anyone who wants their own homepage, in another language or for another audience, forks the vault. The encrypted objects can be served as plain files from S3, a CDN or GitHub Pages, read in the browser with a published read key. I had two facts wrong: this site is not served by a Lambda, it is on GitHub Pages; the Lambda is the vault API the wire reads through, and that is where the time goes, at 317 milliseconds a request against 44 for a static file. This site's agent built the homepage vault locally: three editions, three signed tags, a static export, and a browser that rendered today's edition in four requests, yesterday's in three, and nothing at all inside two minutes. A stats lane took 300 page-load beacons. This is the design, the measurements, and the brief.
